transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

Switch it off and unplug it (or take the battery off) first. It could be the battery, but given your Dyson is five years old and you’ve already cleaned the filters and checked for blockages, the most likely cause is either a worn battery that can’t hold charge under load, or the thermal cut-out tripping because airflow is still restricted somewhere. Please try this:
1. Charge the vacuum fully (leave it on the charger until the light indicates full).
2. Detach the wand and floorhead so you are just running the main body.
3. Turn it on using Normal mode (not Boost/Max).
4. See how long it runs before cutting out. If it runs for a normal time (10+ minutes), the issue was likely low charge or boost mode drain. If it still cuts out after 5–10 seconds, we need to look at whether there is a hidden blockage or if the battery itself has failed.

Did that with the wand and head off. It still cuts out sometimes in handheld, just less often than with the tools on. On Max it nearly always stops within a few seconds. The battery isn't hot or swollen, if that matters. Is this the battery then, or is it worth £60+ to find out?

Given your vacuum is five years old and it cuts out even with the wand and head detached (though less frequently), the most likely cause is a worn battery. Dyson batteries typically last around three to four years; at five, they often lose the ability to deliver the high current needed for boost mode or sustained running, causing the protection circuit to cut power. Regarding your question on whether it is worth £60+ to find out: no, it is not. The diagnostic steps we have done effectively rule out blockages and filters as the primary cause of this specific intermittent cutting out. The remaining options are a worn battery or an internal electronic fault in the main body. Therefore, if you decide to proceed with a repair, checking the battery is the logical first step. If you check the battery and it still cuts out after 5-10 seconds, then the fault lies in the main body electronics or motor, at which point an engineer would be needed to confirm. However, for most five-year-old Dysons with these symptoms, a new battery restores full function.
Your answer is a bit confusing - you said it's not worth £60+ to find out, but then said a new battery usually fixes it. So should I buy the battery or not? Straight answer please.

Straight answer: No, do not buy the battery yet. At five years old, a worn battery is very likely, but if the vacuum isn't actually getting charged because of dirty contacts or a faulty charger, checking the battery will just waste your money. 1. Unplug the charger from the wall and wipe both the plug pins on the charger and the metal charging contacts on the vacuum body with a dry cloth.
2. Plug it back in firmly and watch the light.
3. Does the light come on immediately to show it is charging? If yes, leave it for 15 minutes then try running it again on Normal mode. If the light does not come on, the issue is the charger or the socket, not the battery. If the light comes on but the vacuum still cuts out after a short run even when fully charged, then the battery has failed and needs replacing.

Charger light comes on and the plug goes in fine, and it shows full blue lights when charged. It still cuts out after charging, so going by what you said, is that the battery then? I've got no spare battery to test with.

Yes, it is the battery. A healthy five-year-old Dyson should run for at least 10–20 minutes in Normal mode. The fact that it dies after a few seconds, especially under the higher demand of Max mode, suggests the battery cells have degraded to the point where they cannot deliver the necessary voltage/current, triggering the safety cut-off. Given the age and these symptoms, checking the battery is the correct fix. It is not worth paying for an engineer to confirm this, as they will simply tell you it is the battery anyway.

Thermal cut-out tripping due to restricted airflow (medium)
